title: A Simple Urine Test Can Now Screen Children for Autism. It Measures Gut Bacteria Compounds That Are Up to 1,000 Times Higher in Affected Kids.
excerpt: Researchers at Arizona State University have developed a screening tool that analyses 17 microbial metabolites in urine to identify children at risk of autism spectrum disorder. For Indian-American parents navigating long diagnostic waitlists, this could be transformative.
body:
Getting a child evaluated for autism in America can take anywhere from six months to two years. The average age of diagnosis is four years and four months — well past the window when early intervention is most effective.

A new study published this week in Molecular Psychiatry suggests an alternative: a simple urine test that can identify children at risk of autism spectrum disorder by measuring compounds produced by bacteria in their gut.

The tool, developed by researchers at Arizona State University in collaboration with Harvard Medical School and Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, screens for 17 specific microbial metabolites — small molecules created by microorganisms living in the digestive tract. In a study of 99 children aged 2 to 11, it distinguished between children with autism and those without with high accuracy.

What the Test Found

The researchers collected urine samples from 52 children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder and 47 neurotypical children. Using a classification system they call the Microbially-Derived Metabolite System, or MDM, they scored each sample based on how many metabolites exceeded typical ranges.

The results were unambiguous. Between 80 and 90 per cent of children with autism had extremely elevated levels of at least one microbial metabolite. Some levels were up to 1,000 times higher than anything observed in the control group. On average, children with autism had three elevated metabolites, compared to near-zero in neurotypical children.

The specific compounds that stood out are derived from tyrosine, tryptophan, and phenylalanine — amino acids that serve as building blocks for serotonin and dopamine, two neurotransmitters central to mood, cognition, social behaviour, and attention.

"What's really striking about the bacteria is that they make metabolites that are basically altered versions of serotonin and dopamine," said James Adams, the study's corresponding author and a professor at ASU. These altered neurotransmitter precursors could "explain many of the symptoms and co-occurring symptoms in children with autism — their social communication, anxiety, depression, and attention."

The Gut-Brain Connection in Autism

The study builds on a decade of research connecting gut microbiome imbalances to neurological conditions. Children with autism have long been known to have higher rates of gastrointestinal problems — constipation, diarrhoea, abdominal pain — but the biological mechanism linking gut bacteria to brain development has remained elusive.

This study provides the clearest evidence yet that microbial metabolites may be a measurable, biological marker for autism risk. Unlike behavioural assessments, which depend on subjective observation and vary significantly between clinicians, a urine metabolite test is objective, reproducible, and can be administered by any paediatrician.

The researchers also found compounds linked to yeast and fungal overgrowth in the autism group, suggesting that gut microbiome disruptions in these children extend beyond bacteria.

"Using this test will tell you which young children are at high risk for being diagnosed with autism, and guide treatment in those who have already been diagnosed to help them lead their best lives," said Christina Flynn, the study's first author and a recent ASU PhD graduate.

Why Indian-American Parents Should Watch This

Autism diagnoses in the United States have increased 175 per cent between 2011 and 2022. The CDC currently estimates that 1 in 36 children has autism spectrum disorder.

For immigrant families, the path to diagnosis is often longer and more frustrating. Language barriers, cultural stigma around developmental differences, and unfamiliarity with the American healthcare system all contribute to delayed evaluation. Indian-American children are diagnosed later on average than their white peers, despite evidence that autism prevalence is comparable across ethnic groups.

A urine-based screening test would remove several of those barriers. It requires no specialist referral, no behavioural observation session, and no lengthy waitlist. It can be done at a routine paediatric visit. If validated in larger trials, it could become the first biological screening tool for autism — a condition that has historically been defined entirely by behaviour.

Early intervention — speech therapy, occupational therapy, social skills training — is most effective when started before age three. A screening tool that identifies at-risk children at age two could shift the entire trajectory of a child's development.

The Limitations

The study involved 99 children, which is small. The researchers acknowledge that larger, more diverse studies are needed before the MDM System can be used clinically. The test identifies elevated metabolite levels, not autism itself — it is a screening tool, not a diagnostic one.

There are also questions about what causes the metabolite elevations. Are the gut bacteria different because of autism, or does something about the gut environment contribute to autism's development? The study cannot answer that question, though the researchers believe the causation may run in both directions.

Clinical validation trials are expected to begin within the next year. If they confirm these findings in larger populations, a commercial test could be available within three to five years.

What Parents Can Do Now

The urine test is not yet available commercially. But the research underscores the importance of gut health in childhood development — a connection that Ayurvedic and traditional Indian medicine has emphasised for centuries.

Parents who notice gastrointestinal symptoms alongside developmental concerns should mention both to their paediatrician. The two may be more connected than standard medical practice currently recognises.

If you are waiting for an autism evaluation, do not wait for the evaluation to begin intervention. Speech therapy and occupational therapy are beneficial for a wide range of developmental differences and do not require an autism diagnosis to start.
